## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Time series decomposition

A decomposition model decomposes a time series into multiple components.

Usual components include:

trend ($T$), seasonality ($S$), remainder ($R$)

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why decompose data?

* Explore constituent patterns in a time series
* Seasonal adjustment for long-term decision making
* Simplifies modelling of complex patterns
:::


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposition structure

Decomposition models are usually either

* Additive: $Y = T + S + R$

* Multiplicative: $Y = T \times S \times R$

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout}
## :bulb: The sum of its parts

We can forecast each component independently, then combine to forecast the original series.

::: {.fragment}

Probablistic forecasts are convolutions of additive parts.

$$y_{T+h|T} = T_{T+h|T} + S_{T+h|T} + R_{T+h|T}$$
:::
:::
:::


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### (M)STL Decomposition

**S**easonal and  
**T**rend decomposition using  
**L**oess

::: callout-tip

## Additive decomposition via STL

$$ y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t $$

* $y_t=$ data at time $t$
* $T_t=$ trend-cycle component at time $t$
* $S_t=$ seasonal component at time $t$
* $R_t=$ remainder component at time $t$

:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### (M)STL Decomposition

::: callout-tip
## Advantages

* Handles any seasonality of any periodicity.
* Allows seasonality and trend to change over time.
* Change sensitivity can be tuned via window sizes.
* Optionally robust to outliers.
:::

::: callout-important
## Disadvantages

* Additive decomposition only.
* Simplistic model (no trading day or holiday effects).
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
### Time series components

Consider these (synthetic) components.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)

i <- 1:119
pattern_types_demo <- tsibble(
  time = yearmonth(i),
  season = sin(i*2*pi/12),
  trend = i,
  remainder = rnorm(length(i)),
  index = time
)
pattern_types_demo |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(season, trend, remainder)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = value, group = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(vars(name), scales = "free_y") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/laura-geror-lGeAZjIhQyo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposing multiplicative data

STL can't decompose multiplicative patterns.

This isn't a problem though, since we  
have a *transformational* trick :magic_wand:

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

\begin{aligned}
\log(Y) &= \log(T \times S \times R) \\
        &= \log(T) + \log(S) + \log(R)
\end{aligned}

We must transform multiplicative patterns to additive patterns before STL decomposition.

:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposing multiplicative data

Total Australian retail turnover is multiplicative, so we cannot use STL directly.

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  autoplot(Turnover)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposing multiplicative data

Log transform the data to make multiplicative patterns additive.

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  autoplot(log(Turnover))
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposing multiplicative data

Box-Cox transformations are more flexible.  
$\lambda = 0$ is $f(x) = \log(x)$, $\lambda = 1$ is $f(x) = x$.

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  autoplot(box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2))
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### STL Decomposition

The STL model decomposes a time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components.

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  model(STL(box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2))) |> 
  components()
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### STL Decomposition

`autoplot()` plots the components.

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  model(STL(box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2))) |> 
  components() |> 
  autoplot()
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### STL Decomposition

`window` sizes adjust the fit.

```{r}
#| echo: true
aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  model(STL(box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2) ~ season(window = Inf))) |> 
  components() |> 
  autoplot()
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposition forecasting

Forecast components with simple models, then combine the component forecasts.


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip}
## Seasonal adjustment

We usually model/forecast trend ($T$) and remainder ($R$) together using a single model - this is known seasonally adjusted.

$$
y_{T+h|T} = (T+R)_{T+h|T} + S_{T+h|T}
$$
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/steven-wright-mq8QogEBy00-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposition forecasting

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-width: 7.5
retail_components <- aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover)) |> 
  model(STL(box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2) ~ season(window = Inf))) |> 
  components() |> 
  transmute(`box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2)`, `Seasonally Adjusted (T + R)` = season_adjust, `Seasonality (S)` = season_year) |> 
  pivot_longer(c(`box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2)`, `Seasonally Adjusted (T + R)`, `Seasonality (S)`), names_to = "component")

retail_components |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(vars(component), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y")
```


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposition forecasting

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-width: 7.5
retail_fc_snaive <- retail_components |> 
  filter(component == "Seasonality (S)") |> 
  model(SNAIVE(value)) |> 
  forecast(h = "2 years") |> 
  mutate(component = "Seasonality (S)")

retail_components |> 
  filter(Month > yearmonth("2010 Jan")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  autolayer(retail_fc_snaive) +
  facet_wrap(vars(component), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y")
```


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

```{r}
retail_fc_ets <- retail_components |> 
  filter(component == "Seasonally Adjusted (T + R)") |>
```

## {}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposition forecasting

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-width: 7.5
retail_fc_dcmp <- retail_components |> 
  filter(component == "box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2)") |> 
  model(    
    decomposition_model(
      dcmp = STL(value ~ season(window = Inf)),
      ETS(season_adjust),
      SNAIVE(season_year)
    )
  ) |> 
  forecast(h = "2 years") |> 
  mutate(component = "box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2)")

retail_components |> 
  filter(Month > yearmonth("2010 Jan")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  autolayer(retail_fc_snaive) +
  autolayer(retail_fc_ets) +
  autolayer(retail_fc_dcmp) +
  facet_wrap(vars(component), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y")
```


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Convolutions of forecasts

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
retail_fc_snaive
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
cat("# A fable: 24 x 4 [1M]
# Key:     component, .model [1]
   component      .model    Month       value
   <chr>          <chr>     <mth>      <dist>
 1 Seasonality (… SNAIV… 2019 Jan N(-0.13, 0)
 2 Seasonality (… SNAIV… 2019 Feb N(-0.79, 0)
 3 Seasonality (… SNAIV… 2019 Mar N(-0.17, 0)
 4 Seasonality (… SNAIV… 2019 Apr N(-0.36, 0)
# ℹ 20 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: .mean <dbl>
# ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows")
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=2}
::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
retail_fc_ets
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
cat("# A fable: 24 x 5 [1M]
# Key:     component, .model [1]
   component      .model    Month        value
   <chr>          <chr>     <mth>       <dist>
 1 Seasonally Ad… ETS(v… 2019 Jan N(39, 0.019)
 2 Seasonally Ad… ETS(v… 2019 Feb N(39, 0.021)
 3 Seasonally Ad… ETS(v… 2019 Mar N(39, 0.022)
 4 Seasonally Ad… ETS(v… 2019 Apr N(39, 0.023)
# ℹ 20 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: .mean <dbl>
# ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows")
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=4}
::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=2}
These forecasts are normally distributed:

$$S_{T+h|T} \sim N(\mu_{S,T+h}, \sigma_{S,T+h}^2)$$

$$(T+R)_{T+h|T} \sim N(\mu_{T+R,T+h}, \sigma_{T+R,T+h}^2)$$
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=3}
The combined forecast is a convolution.

$$Y_{T+h|T} = S_{T+h|T} + (T+R)_{T+h|T}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=4}
If the forecasts are independent:
$$Y_{T+h|T} \sim N(\mu_{T+R,T+h} + \mu_{S,T+h},\ \sigma_{T+R,T+h}^2 + \sigma_{S,T+h}^2)$$
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=5}
If they're **not** independent:

$$E(Y_{T+h|T}) = \mu_{T+R,T+h} + \mu_{S,T+h}$$

$$\text{Var}(Y_{T+h|T}) = \sigma_{T+R,T+h}^2 + \sigma_{S,T+h}^2 + 2\sigma_{T+R,S,T+h}$$
:::


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Convolutions of forecasts

The PDF of $Z = X + Y$ is a convolution of:

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: callout
## 🎲 Independent variables

Marginal densities are sufficient:

$$f_Z(z) = (f_X * f_Y)(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\, f_Y(z - x)\, dx$$
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: callout
## 🔗 Dependent variables

The joint density is required:

$$f_Z(z) = f_{X,Y}(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,\, z - x)\, dx$$
:::
:::



:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Convolutions of forecasts

When a single seasonal window is used, $S_{T+h|T}$ and $(T+R)_{T+h|T}$ are independent.

[Since `window = Inf`, the seasonality is constant and seasonal naive exactly predicts the seasonal component (0 variance).]{.fragment .fade-up}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We can convolve these distributions together:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
retail_fc_snaive$value[2]
```
:::

::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
retail_fc_ets$value[2]
```
:::

:::


:::
::: {.fragment .fade-up}
```{r}
#| echo: true
retail_fc_snaive$value[1] + retail_fc_ets$value[1]
```
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Convolutions of forecasts

In `fable`, combinations of Gaussian forecasts use correlations between components.


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: callout
## 🔢 Covariance structure

$\Sigma = DRD$

Where

* $R$ is the correlation matrix, and
* $D$ is a diagonal matrix of forecast standard deviations.

:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: callout
## 🔔 Gaussian copulas

This is closely related to Gaussian copulas. 

The correlation matrix is estimated from the joint response residuals of component models.
:::

:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Back-transforming forecasts

Lastly, we must undo the transformation to produce forecasts on the original scale.

::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=1}
::: {.callout}
## 🔄 Transforming distributions

If $X \sim F$ and $X = g(Y)$, then the PDF of $Y$ is:

$$f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \left| \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) \right|$$
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=2}
::: {.callout}

## 📐 Example: back-transforming $log(Y) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$

If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and $X = \log(Y)$, then $g^{-1}(y) = e^y$ and $\frac{d}{dy}e^y = e^y$,

$$f_Y(y) = f_X(e^y) \cdot e^y = \frac{1}{y\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\log y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$

i.e. $Y \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.
:::
:::

## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Back-transforming forecasts

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 7
library(ggdist)
library(distributional)

mu <- 0.3
sigma2 <- 0.5

data.frame(
  dist = c(dist_normal(mu, sqrt(sigma2)), dist_lognormal(mu, sqrt(sigma2))),
  label = c(
    "X = log(Y) ~ N(\u03bc, \u03c3\u00b2)",
    "Y ~ LogNormal(\u03bc, \u03c3\u00b2)"
  )
) |>
  ggplot(aes(xdist = dist, y = label)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  stat_halfeye(point_interval = mean_qi, .width = c(0.5, 0.95)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(mu), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = mu + 0.05, xend = exp(mu) - 0.05,
    y = 1.5, yend = 1.5,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), ends = "last", type = "closed")
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = (mu + exp(mu)) / 2, y = 1.56,
    label = "Y = e^X",
    hjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, colour = "grey20", fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = mu, y = 0.6,
    label = sprintf("\u03bc = %.1f", mu),
    hjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = exp(mu), y = 0.6,
    label = sprintf("e^\u03bc = %.2f", exp(mu)),
    hjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.5, 5)) + 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Back-transforming forecasts

```{=html}
<style>
.math {
  padding-right: 0 !important;
}
</style>
```

::: {.callout}

## ⚖️ "Bias adjustment"

Quantiles (incl. medians) can be directly back-transformed:

$$Q_p(Y) = g^{-1}(Q_p(X))$$

**However**, the mean does not back-transform directly:

$$E(Y) = E[g^{-1}(X)] \neq g^{-1}(E[X])$$

::: {.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=1}
For $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, a 2nd-order Taylor expansion gives:

$$E[g^{-1}(X)] \approx g^{-1}(\mu) + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \cdot (g^{-1})''(\mu)$$

For $g^{-1}(x) = e^x$, this is exact: $E(Y) = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$

Larger $\sigma^2$ $\Rightarrow$ bigger correction.

:::

:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

### Back-transforming forecasts

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 7
library(ggdist)
library(distributional)

mu <- 0.3
sigma2 <- 0.5

data.frame(
  dist = c(dist_normal(mu, sqrt(sigma2)), dist_lognormal(mu, sqrt(sigma2))),
  label = c(
    "X = log(Y) ~ N(\u03bc, \u03c3\u00b2)",
    "Y ~ LogNormal(\u03bc, \u03c3\u00b2)"
  )
) |>
  ggplot(aes(xdist = dist, y = label)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  stat_halfeye(point_interval = mean_qi, .width = c(0.5, 0.95)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(mu), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(mu + sigma2/2), linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = mu + 0.05, xend = exp(mu) - 0.05,
    y = 1.5, yend = 1.5,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), ends = "last", type = "closed")
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = (mu + exp(mu)) / 2, y = 1.56,
    label = "Y = e^X",
    hjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, colour = "grey20", fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = mu + 0.05, xend = exp(mu + sigma2/2) - 0.05,
    y = 1.2, yend = 1.2,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), ends = "last", type = "closed"),
    colour = "steelblue"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = (mu + exp(mu + sigma2/2)) / 2, y = 1.27,
    label = "E(Y) == e^{mu + sigma^2/2}",
    parse = TRUE,
    hjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, colour = "steelblue", fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = mu, y = 0.6,
    label = sprintf("\u03bc = %.1f", mu),
    hjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = exp(mu + sigma2/2), y = 0.6,
    label = sprintf("E(Y) = %.2f", exp(mu + sigma2/2)),
    hjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, colour = "steelblue"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.5, 5)) +
```

## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Decomposition forecasting

Decomposition forecasts are specified with:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
decomposition_model(
  dcmp = `decomposition`,
  ... # (models for each component)
)
```


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout}
## 🔧 `decomposition_model()` handles everything

* **decomposition** of the original series,
* **forecasting** each decomposed component,
* **convolution** to combine forecasts with covariance,
* **back-transformation** of forecasts to original scale.
:::
:::


:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {.fragment-remove}

::: columns

::: {.column width="60%"}


The Australian retail forecasts were:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
decomposition_model(
  dcmp = STL(box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2) ~ season(window = Inf)),
  ETS(season_adjust),
  SNAIVE(season_year)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
aus_retail_tot <- aus_retail |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover))
aus_retail_tot |> 
  model(    
    decomposition_model(
      dcmp = STL(box_cox(Turnover, lambda = 0.2) ~ season(window = Inf)),
      ETS(season_adjust),
      SNAIVE(season_year)
    )
  ) |> 
  forecast(h = "2 years") |> 
  autoplot(aus_retail_tot)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/roberto-sorin-RS0-h_pyByk-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}
